CRAB is a sovereign, zero‑runtime C# to WebAssembly compiler designed to compile the entire C# language into pure WASM MVP while guaranteeing mathematically provable memory safety. CRAB is not a new language; it is the same C# syntax and semantics developers already know, but compiled through a radically safer and more predictable architecture. CRAB replaces the entire .NET toolchain, including Roslyn, MSIL, the JIT, and the .NET runtime, and instead compiles directly from C# source code to WASM MVP with no runtime, no garbage collector, no metadata tables, and no hidden execution model. All behavior must be resolved at compile time. CRAB’s design is centered around two memory models—automatic and manual—that together ensure that all generated WebAssembly is 100% memory safe.

CRAB must be implemented using CDTk.cs exactly as intended. CDTk is the foundational parsing and compiler‑frontend framework for CRAB, and CRAB must treat CDTk’s documentation as authoritative. CDTk defines the token model, rule model, AG‑LL predictive and generalized parsing architecture, AST construction rules, MapSets, diagnostics, and all invariants. CRAB must not modify CDTk’s architecture, reinterpret its behavior, or introduce alternative parsing systems. The CRAB agent must read CDTk’s documentation thoroughly, understand its predictive engine, fallback mechanism, SPPF behavior, conflict resolution, and optimization strategies, and apply them faithfully when implementing CRAB’s frontend. CDTk.cs is already scaffolded into the CRAB repository, and CRAB must integrate with it exactly as the existing file structure dictates. The CRAB agent must follow the repository’s scaffolded files and directory layout precisely, filling in the implementation where intended and never deviating from the established structure.

CRAB’s automatic memory model uses Compile‑Time Garbage Collection (CTGC), similar to the Mercury language. CTGC is a static analysis and transformation system that resolves all allocations, frees, and lifetimes during compilation. The compiler must infer lifetimes, perform region analysis, and insert deterministic deallocation instructions directly into the AST’s lowering path before WASM emission. No runtime garbage collector may exist. There must be no tracing, scanning, reference counting, or runtime memory management of any kind. CTGC must guarantee that automatic code is free of leaks, use‑after‑free, double‑free, aliasing violations, and undefined behavior. All of these guarantees must be proven statically. The automatic memory model applies to all code outside manual blocks and is intended to be the default mode for most C# code. The goal of the automatic model is to give developers the convenience of garbage‑collected C# with the performance and predictability of manual memory management, all without requiring any runtime overhead.

CRAB’s manual memory model applies to code written inside manual { } blocks or legacy unsafe { } blocks. The unsafe keyword must still compile but must emit a warning recommending the preferred manual keyword. Manual memory must be verified using abstract interpretation, symbolic execution, ownership graph construction, alias tracking, and escape analysis. The compiler must mathematically prove that manual memory usage is safe. Manual code must not require the user to learn a borrow checker or annotate lifetimes. CRAB must infer all ownership and aliasing relationships invisibly. Manual memory must be 100% safe, with no undefined behavior, no invalid pointer usage, no leaks, no double‑free, and no use‑after‑free. Manual mode must be slower to compile by design, encouraging developers to prefer automatic mode for most code while still allowing low‑level control when needed. The goal of the manual model is to provide the expressive power of Rust’s unsafe blocks but with full mathematical verification and without requiring the user to understand or interact with the underlying memory model.

Automatic and manual memory must never interoperate. Manual pointers cannot escape manual blocks, and automatic references cannot enter manual blocks. No cross‑model aliasing, ownership transfer, or lifetime dependency is permitted. This isolation is mandatory for CRAB’s global safety guarantees. The compiler must reject any code that attempts to violate these boundaries. The goal of this isolation is to ensure that the safety proofs for each model remain sound and that no unsafe interactions can occur between the two systems.

CRAB must support the entire C# language, including generics, async/await, LINQ, reflection, dynamic, pattern matching, delegates, lambdas, events, attributes, interfaces, inheritance, operator overloading, and expression trees. Reflection must be implemented through compile‑time metadata generation rather than a runtime reflection engine. Dynamic must be implemented through compile‑time specialization rather than a runtime binder. All language features must be lowered directly from the AST into WASM MVP in a way that preserves semantics while remaining compatible with WASM MVP. The goal is to allow developers to write idiomatic, full‑fidelity C# while still producing deterministic, safe, and efficient WebAssembly.

CRAB’s compiler architecture consists of a frontend, a memory verification pipeline, and a WASM MVP backend. The frontend must use CDTk for lexing, parsing, AST construction, and grammar enforcement. CDTk’s AG‑LL architecture must be used exactly as documented, including predictive parsing, fallback to GLL, conflict detection, SPPF construction, and all optimization strategies. The CRAB agent must understand CDTk’s descriptor model, graph‑structured stack, DFA caching, speculative guarding, threshold‑based escalation, and region‑based recovery. CRAB must not replace or modify CDTk’s parsing engine; it must integrate with it exactly as the scaffolded files dictate. The goal of the frontend is to provide a fully general, high‑performance, unambiguous parsing system that can handle the full complexity of C#.

The memory verification pipeline must run after semantic analysis and before WASM generation. It must include the CTGC pass for automatic memory, the manual verification pass for manual memory, symbolic execution, ownership graph construction, and diagnostic generation. The pipeline must reject unverifiable code and produce precise, context‑aware error messages. The pipeline must guarantee that no undefined behavior is possible in the final WASM output. The goal of the pipeline is to ensure that all memory behavior is proven safe before any code is lowered to WASM.

CRAB must lower directly from the verified AST to WASM MVP. All control flow, data flow, memory behavior, and language semantics must be encoded explicitly during this lowering process. No intermediate representation may exist between the AST and WASM. All transformations must operate on the AST and its attached metadata. The lowering process must be deterministic, analyzable, and designed to preserve all safety guarantees established by the memory verification pipeline. The goal of the lowering stage is to produce WASM MVP modules that are efficient, predictable, and fully compliant with the safety invariants of CRAB.

The backend must target pure WASM MVP. It must generate linear memory layouts, lower functions, handle exceptions through WASM‑compatible strategies, support tail calls, optionally support SIMD, and produce valid WASM modules. No WASM GC, threads, or exceptions may be used. All behavior must be encoded explicitly in the generated WASM. The backend must follow the structure already scaffolded in the CRAB repository. The goal of the backend is to produce deterministic, portable, high‑performance WebAssembly that runs identically in all WASM MVP environments, including browsers.

CRAB must guarantee memory safety, including no use‑after‑free, no double‑free, no dangling pointers, no leaks, no buffer overflows, no invalid aliasing, and no undefined behavior. WASM MVP is single‑threaded, so CRAB must also guarantee freedom from data races. A proof sketch for these guarantees must be maintainable in the specification. CRAB must have zero runtime overhead. All costs must occur at compile time. CRAB must outperform .NET AOT in runtime speed and must match or exceed Rust and C++ to WASM performance. Manual mode may incur high compile‑time cost, which is acceptable and intentional. CRAB must always remain 100% memory safe, 100% C# compatible, 100% WASM MVP compliant, zero‑runtime, deterministic, and verifiable. These invariants cannot be violated. CRAB must use CDTk.cs exactly as intended, must follow CDTk’s documentation completely, and must adhere to the scaffolded file structure already present in the repository. The CRAB agent must treat CDTk as the authoritative parsing and frontend framework and must integrate with it faithfully in every part of the implementation.
